title: Korte en lange klinkers
intro: Dutch vowels come in short and long pairs. A doubled letter (aa, ee, oo, uu) is long. A single vowel is also long when it ends a syllable: ja, nu, zo, ze-ven. Before a double consonant it is short: hebben, stoppen.

rows.d: Short and clipped, made at the back of the mouth. Shorter and darker than the a in “father”.
Long, like the a in “father”.
Short, like the e in “bed”.
Long, like “ay” in “day” but held steady, without sliding into an “ee” at the end.

An unstressed e sounds like the a in “about” (a schwa). In longer words this is the e of -je, ge- and -en; the n of -en is often dropped. Short words do it too: de, je, we, ze, een, and het is usually said ’t. A beginner's guideline, not a rule for every unstressed e.
Short, like the i in “bit”.
Like the ee in “see”, but shorter.
Short, like the o in British “hot”.
Long, like the o in “go” but held steady, without the “w” glide at the end.
Short, with no English match: say the i in “bit” with slightly rounded lips.
Long: round your lips as for “oo” and say “ee”. Like French tu.

title: Klinkercombinaties
intro: These letter pairs each make one sound. ij and ei sound exactly the same.

rows.d: Like the oo in “food”.
Start with the e of “bed” and glide towards “ee”. Close to “ay” in “day”, but opening wider.
No English match. Round your lips and say the “ow” of “house” with your tongue forward. Practise this one slowly.
Like the “ow” in “how”.
Say the “ay” of “day” with your lips rounded, and hold it. Like French deux.
The vowel plus a short “y” glide at the end.
From the back of the throat, like the ch in Scottish “loch”. In the Netherlands g and ch sound the same.
An s followed by that same throat sound: s + ch.
Like the y in “yes”, never like the English j.
Softer than English w. Your lower lip lightly touches your upper teeth, between a v and a w.
At the start of a word it often sounds almost like an f.
Either rolled or made in the throat, and it varies by region. After a vowel at the end of a word it is often soft.
At the end of a word, d sounds like t and b sounds like p.
In everyday speech the final n is usually dropped: hebben sounds like “hebbe”.
The unstressed ending sounds like “-uch” with the throat ch.

title: Klemtoon en let op
intro: Most Dutch words stress the first syllable. The prefixes be-, ge- and her- are never stressed: be-DANKT, be-GRIJ-pen, ge-DAAN, her-HA-len. The accents in één show it is said with a full, stressed ee, which separates “one” from “a”.

rows.d: een (“a”) sounds like “un”. één (“one”) has the long ee.
13–19 end in -tien (“teen”), 30–90 end in -tig.
jij, wij, zij are stressed forms. je, we, ze are the everyday, unstressed forms.
Unstressed prefix, stress on the next syllable.

title: Zinnen
intro: Words change when they run together. Listen for the rhythm.

ex: Hoi, hoe gaat het?|Hi, how are you?
Goed, dank je. En met jou?|Fine, thanks. And you?
Ik heet Steven.|My name is Steven.
Waar kom je vandaan?|Where are you from?
Waar woon je?|Where do you live?
Tot de volgende les!|See you next class!
